items.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007
items.q: And then of course the Bing Crosby, the pop. Not swing but the pop tunes.

ctx.x: But it has a groove to it.

It’s just, you hear it. There’s nothing but rhythm going on. I still have some Romanian LPs you know. It’s outasight. It’s a sense of rhythm and you know like odd tempos in seven and five and you know. Well so anyhow, I was exposed to this Hungarian music. And then I was exposed to the swing era, you know swing music, the big bands you know, that business [scats] sophisticated swing you know. I have a vivid memory of walking through a carnival kind of thing, an outdoor thing, with my mother, late at night. ©…

Maybe we were walking to go home or something, I don’t know how. And over the P.A. system came that. And I liked that, and I said yeah. Years later when I heard it I said ooh I know that. So I was exposed to swing, I was exposed to Hungarian music, and then in that area there was a station, WWVA, and it had the equivalent of Grand Ole Opry. And on Saturday a midnight jamboree or something you know. And they had country players and fiddles and banjos and stuff. And so I had that influence. And so that was country-…
